title: Why Doesn't the Heart Symbol Look Like a Heart?
parts: You draw it on cards, on cakes, on text messages.
Two curves, a point at the bottom.
No real heart looks like that.
The real organ has four chambers, and no notch at the top.
So where did this shape come from?
At least four explanations compete for the answer.
We'll mark every one: documented, disputed, or myth.
By the end, you'll know exactly what historians can date, and what they can't.
And you'll see the real mystery isn't the shape — it's who drew it first, and why.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
Here's what the historical record actually shows.
Early in the thirteen hundreds, artists started drawing a dented shape for the heart.
One writer, Francesco da Barberino, used it before thirteen twenty, in a book called Documenti d'amore.
At first, it was only lightly dented — barely different from a plain oval.
A painter named Giotto comes even earlier.
Around thirteen oh five, in a chapel in Padua, he painted a figure named Charity handing her own heart to Christ.
That heart looks anatomical — not the dented shape we use today.
Documented: the image exists, dated, in a real chapel.
Some push the date back even further, to the twelve fifties.
A poem called the Romance of the Pear describes a heart-shaped object.
But the source itself calls that reading "dubious" — it might just be a pear.
Disputed, as the earliest example.
The shape kept evolving through the thirteen thirties, in sculpture by Andrea Pisano.
It rounded out over the following century.
By the late fourteen hundreds, this exact shape shows up printed on playing cards.
A historian named Knutson dates that use precisely.
Documented: from a lightly dented oval to the suit symbol, on paper we can still read today.
So the timeline of the shape itself is solid.
What's not solid is why anyone chose this shape in the first place.
Four theories try to answer that — and none of them has a clean paper trail.
Theory one: an extinct plant called silphium.
Ancient coins from the city of Cyrene, more than two thousand years old, show a seed shape close to our symbol.
Silphium was one of the most valuable plants of the ancient world.
Some writers link its seed shape directly to the heart symbol.
But historians call that link speculative — the coin is real, the connection isn't proven.
Theory two is that same old pear from the twelve-fifty poem, read again as the true origin.
Theory three points to ivy or water-lily leaves in medieval art and heraldry.
Both show up in art history.
Neither one has a source that actually proves it started the symbol.
Theory four reads the shape as parts of the human body.
One modern writer, in nineteen ninety-eight, called it a likely echo of something older.
Historians say there's no documented line connecting any ancient precedent to the medieval art that actually started this shape.
One historian argues something different entirely.
He suggests medieval illustrators were trying to combine two old, competing descriptions of the heart's own anatomy, and the compromise drawing became our symbol.
It's one argument, from one book — not a settled answer.
Myth, if anyone tells you this mystery is solved.
So the shape's timeline is documented: thirteen hundreds to playing cards, step by step.
But who drew it first, and why, is still four competing guesses.
Our reading: a symbol doesn't need to look like the real thing — it only needs to be easy to draw and easy to recognize.
Which raises an older question: why did people once believe we think, and feel, with the heart at all?
